segments: The fifty-first dynasty.
The Hun kings.
and to his eldest son, he who was the son-in-law of the King of the Armenians.
And on his departure, he put to the edge of the sword the Christians of the city of Roman,
because it was told to him:
"The Tatars are strengthened by these whenever they cross over into Syria."
And as soon as the King of Kings arrived in the territory of the Romans,
he found no one of the Egyptians there,
except certain of the Turkmens
who were fleeing to Syria.
He overtook and killed them,
and took their families captive.
And the Tatars, in their greed,
were killing, taking captive, and plundering many of the Christians as well,
even though the King of Kings {OCR?} had commanded that they should not harm the Christians,
because they had hidden and sustained many of the Tatars who had escaped from the Egyptians.
For he also gave a yarlikh into the hands of a certain priest and a monk,
and ordered them to go around through the camps
and deliver the Christian prisoners from the territory of the Romans.
And thus they indeed did.
And when the King of Kings had gone around through the mountains of Cappadocia
and reached the place called Aqsha (or Aghja? Darband),
he turned back again.
And when the Pervaneh came to the King of Kings,
he did not diminish his honor at all,
but rather exalted him greatly.
And he took him with him,
as if to make arrangements concerning the territory of the Romans,
and how much force,
and which commander they should leave there,
who would be able to stand against the Egyptian,
if he should again repeat his invasion.
And when they reached Armenia,
at the mountain called Alatağ,
he made a banquet for the Pervaneh,
and gave him much mares' milk to drink,
because he did not drink wine.
And when he went out to pass water,
the King of Kings motioned {OCR?} to the armed men,
and they hacked him limb from limb on the second day of the week (Monday),
on the second day of the month of Ab of that same year,
which is the year one thousand five hundred and eighty-eight of the Greeks [1277 AD],
six hundred and seventy-five of the Arabs [675 AH].
And thus, by the death with which he had put to death Sultan Rukn al-Din,
he himself was also put to death,
so that there might be fulfilled that saying:
"The murderer shall be killed,
and his blood shall not be counted."
It is said
that as soon as they drew swords against him,
he was not shaken nor was he terrified,
but cast foul curses at the Tatars, saying:
"Is this my recompense from you,
and the recompense of all"
